title: Peter praised alone, then doubled by Paul
english: The rose is beautiful, and springtime gives it its scent to breathe. Joined with the lily, it rightly grows still more fragrant. Ointment is mixed with ointment, and the pleasure of the scent is doubled. Peter shines by himself, and he outshines the bright. He is the chief of the apostolic pair, the eye of discipleship, the living record of zeal and the face of faith. He is the trumpet of the mystery, the tongue that taught many tongues, the blameless shepherd, the sleepless pilot, the charioteer who never strays, the pharmacist who prepared the lasting salve of repentance.

He is the fisherman of the sea, and his fish are caught for heaven. His net holds miracles for its threads, sufferings for its bait, the cross for its hook, and the resurrection for its embrace. He is the keeper of the keys of the storehouse where the Father keeps his treasures, the Son his bridal chambers, the Spirit his table, and the angels their dances.

But with Paul added, the wall is doubled and cannot be taken. The spring has two mouths and waters the whole earth without wearying. The lake has two faces, and every vessel sailing past it is saved. The turtledove speaks with the swallow, the dove answers the grasshopper, and the flute and the pipe together sing a holy and gentle song. A young man with a holy man, and their road is straight, as the wise man proclaimed in Proverbs. The lamb and the wolf graze together, and the shepherd is glorified, and the wonders of the wonderworker are crowned. The bull and the lion feed in one pasture, and praises are reaped for the one who gave strength to the bull and bridled the lion. Was not Paul a lion when he was Saul? He scattered the flock by murdering, he terrified the shepherds, he roared inside Jerusalem and frightened the cities. He stirred up the marketplaces and emptied the fields. He never stopped dragging men and women to prison and binding them (Acts 8:3). Yet he was defeated by the endurance of the men and proved weaker than the courage of the women. He ran for nothing, for he did not finish the road. He boxed in vain, for he bloodied his knuckles but could not find his opponent.

So Christ came by, for he is both wise and good. He used gentleness and set aside the high things to put forward the lowly. He did not kindle fire, he did not stir whirlwinds, he did not shake the foundations of the mountains. He did not bare the two-edged sword of an angel. He called with a gentle and loving voice. Christ says, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" (Acts 9:4) What wealth did I take from you? What glory did I strip from you?

translator_notes: Greek: τὰ θαύματα, τὰ παθήματα δέλεαρ — the wonders, the sufferings bait
orientation: The preacher begins the homily by praising Peter and then argues that Paul joins him as the second of the pair.
